O.etym: From Middle English O, o, from Old English o, from Latin o and Ancient Greek ὦ (ô, interjection). Featured prominently in William Tyndale's 1525 translation of the New Testament.

g: The vocative particle, used for direct address.
x: O Death! O Death! Won't you spare me over till another year? - part of the refrain from the American folk song "A Conversation with Death".

c. 1810-1820?, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Notes on Macbeth
O! the affecting beauty of the death of Cawdor, and the presentimental speech of the king: […]
“Lift up your head and your heart, O King. We must follow after this dreadnought, hard on her tracks.”

g: The name of the Latin script letter O/o.
A zero (used in reading out numbers).
x: It is currently two-o-five in the afternoon (2:05 PM).
The first permanent English settlement in America was in Jamestown in sixteen-o-seven (1607).
